body_markdown:
Entry-level Mercedes-Benz models have it tough in North America. The brand has a certain mystique to live up to in the U.S. in particular, where the name has long stood for world-class luxury and impressive performance.


Meanwhile, in Europe, the three-pointed star logo adorns everything from delivery vans to long-haul semi-trucks, bare-boned taxicabs and teensy city hatchbacks. Abroad, the new electric CLA-Class has to be a decent, premium-class EV sedan. Here, customers expect an S-Class experience, shrunk down like a wool sweater pulled fresh from the clothes dryer.


Launched anew for the 2026 model year, the CLA-Class now enters its third generation, this time deviating from its larger siblings in some important ways. You may recall that upscale EVs like the EQE and EQS were shaped like industrial-sized suppositories and stuffed with futuristic, hyper-techy interior touches. Not the case here: The new CLA keeps it all simpler and more conventional, while still looking and feeling like a modern Mercedes. It drives better than most modern Mercedes, too.


### Specs: 2027 Mercedes-Benz CLA 350 4MATIC


• **Price:** $51,400 / $67,300 (base/as-tested)
• **Powertrain:** 85-kWh lithium-ion battery; twin permanently excited synchronous electric motors (one per axle, two-speed automatic transmission on the rear)
• **Horsepower:** 349 hp
• **Torque:** 380 lb-ft
• **Layout:** All-wheel-drive, four-door, five-passenger sedan
• **EPA-Rated Fuel Economy:** 120/115/118 MPGe (city/hwy/combined)
• **Range:** 312 miles
• **0–60 mph:** 4.8 seconds
• **Competitors:** Tesla Model 3, Hyundai Ioniq 6, BMW i4


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes-Benz AG


The CLA’s new architecture is dubbed MMA, not because it knees you in the solar plexus, but because its “Mercedes Modular Architecture” accommodates both electric and combustion power. That matters because the CLA is available as either a pure EV or a hybrid, and the two versions are all but indistinguishable from the outside. Commendably, Mercedes did not feel compelled to make the electric one look “different” or “cutting-edge,” which so many automakers can’t seem to resist. The CLA’s design is less bold and swoopy than in the past, but the styling is still sleek, its lines tidy. Nothing jaw-dropping, but a bit more attractive than the sexless-bean appearance of, say, the brand’s EQ electrics.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Mercedes offers the electric CLA in two flavors: the rear-drive CLA 250+ and the all-wheel-drive 350 4Matic. Our test car was the latter, packing 349 horsepower and 380 lb-ft of torque, courtesy of an electric motor on each axle and an 800-volt, 85-kWh lithium-ion battery. The window sticker began with a starting price of $51,400, but didn’t stay there for long; you step up into a Benz for those nice-to-have features, *and oh, that’s gonna cost ya* . The breakdown:


- Flat, urbane paint shade called Alpine Gray ($1750)
- 19-inch AMG multi-spoke wheels with black accents ($900)
- Sky Control for panoramic roof ($1050)
- Burmester 3D Surround Sound ($880)
- MB.Drive Assist ($1950)
- AMG Line Plus w/Night Package ($3100)
- Pinnacle Line ($5850)


All told, we end up at $67,330. Despite the fancy doo-dads—huge MBUX Superscreen, Augmented Reality navigation projected onto the heads-up display, active ambient lighting, et cetera—the CLA is calm and peaceful inside in a way that is deeply refreshing compared with MB’s laser-arcade cabins of the last five-or-so years. Though not as austere as a Tesla Model 3, Mercedes says the CLA’s cabin design “follows the principle of reduction to the essentials.”


Mercedes-Benz AG


For the record, there’s nothing “essential” about a gigantic screen on which your oily fingers must navigate climate controls (and even lumbar support!), but there is a pleasantly open, uncluttered feel to this interior. A big part of that is the huge glass roof, which lets in a lot of light. That glass is heat-insulated and, when equipped with Sky Control, can impress your friends with an on-command, liquid-crystal transition from transparent to opaque. The new car’s 1.6 inches of added length, along with a more classic sedan profile rather than a fast roofline, allow for improved headroom. Space up front is generous, but six-footers still may not be comfortable in the second row.


Mercedes-Benz AG


Before we get to drive impressions, we need to revisit the CLA’s ancestor, the 190. When it launched in the mid-1980s, it was Mercedes’ first real stab at a compact sedan. Though American critics balked at the hefty price when it was first announced (just under $24,000, or about $77,000 today), many were won over by its engineering and execution: “This wasn’t a new automobile so much as a perfect seven-eighths-scale model of the acclaimed S-class cars,” wrote *Car and Driver* of the 1984 190E 2.3, calling it “a meticulously crafted new breed of Mercedes so complete, so refined, so tightly integrated, so totally Mercedes-Benz that they present the impression that they have been hand-carved out of an ingot of chrome-molybdenum steel.”


Mercedes-Benz AG


The new CLA is no longer a convincingly scaled-down S, but like the 190, it is most definitely a new breed of Mercedes. We do not hesitate to call it the best-driving Benz currently in production, aside from that always-incredible S-Class. The chassis, for starters, is outstanding: nimble in corners, effortless to maneuver around the city, comfortable and composed in virtually all situations. The steering even feels pretty natural. Torque from the electric motors is immediate, with the 268-hp rear axle unit only needing assistance from the 107-hp front unit under high-throttle or low-traction conditions. There is a two-speed transmission on the rear motor, with the second gear engaging at highway speed for greater efficiency. We never once noticed it operating, which is a good thing.


There is work to be done, however, with the brakes. At no point during our week behind the wheel did we ever get used to decelerating, whether it was using the foot pedal or switching between the various regenerative modes. There exists a Goldilocks tune that Mercedes engineers have yet to find, but for the time being there is often too much, too little, or simply inconsistent braking force in any given situation. It’s a glaring weakness in an otherwise picture-perfect driving experience for a premium city car. Even on this higher-performance version of the CLA, Mercedes erred on the side of comfort rather than sportiness—which we’d assert is the right call.


Eric Weiner


Other shortcomings: the screens and various light elements are so bright at night that, amid darkness and rain, the driver is too blinded to see much of anything in the side mirrors. Rear visibility is sub-par thanks to the small size and particular shape of the rear glass. The seats aren’t all that comfortable, which should be table stakes in a Mercedes, and the physical controls on the door feel cheap and awkward to use. The in-house AI “assistant” is about as helpful as a third elbow, insisting on turning on the overhead lamp when we asked it to adjust the brightness of the heads-up display.


Eric Weiner


Beyond that, this is a convincing luxury car—more so than an Audi A3, for sure. The cabin is whisper quiet even at highway speed, and the Burmester speakers probably offer the most powerful, fullest sound of any car in this class. A Tesla Model 3 may have superior infotainment software and sportier handling, but the Benz is more upscale by a mile.


Mercedes-Benz AG


As an EV, the CLA has a lot going for it as well. The 350+ model’s 312 miles of EPA-rated range is more than enough to be useful for regular driving, or even highway duty. Amid several trips to and from Detroit, from our office in Ann Arbor, Michigan, we experienced no huge drop-off in expected range, which can sometimes be the case with freeway-speed driving in EVs. We mostly kept the battery on a slow trickle of 110V power at home, plus a few shorter top-offs on 240V Level 2 power around town, and one DC fast-charging session. Mercedes says the 800-volt system can “significantly reduce charging time in conjunction with the new-generation battery. DC fast charging up to 320 kW enables up to 202 miles of range to be added in as little as ten minutes.” That, however, may require optimal conditions—when charging from 58 percent on a 60-degree day, we saw a maximum of 82 kW from one of Electrify America’s DC fast chargers, which was supposedly capable of 350 kW.


Eric Weiner


Eric Weiner


This new electric CLA is impressive, especially the rear-drive 250+ model’s rated range of 374 miles. And none of the blemishes we mentioned are beyond fixing, though they’d require more than over-the-air updates. Pricing isn’t cheap, though it is a Mercedes, after all, and the upcoming BMW i3 promises to be even more expensive. But this chassis! Downright brilliant for around-town cruising or a basic commute, and the electric powertrain is more polished than the workaday gas engines in preceding CLA generations. (We hope the new CLA 220 hybrid proves as astute.) Mercedes should take note: Whatever magic it did with this MMA platform, scale that *up* to the rest of the showroom.
